This measure upgrade models cellulose as the drill-and-fill insulation material. Drill-and-fill insulation can be installed from either the inside or outside of the building. In multifamily buildings, drilling from the outside is more common because it allows occupants to remain in place during the work is being performed, and reduces asbestos risk for installers (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 2011) (Antonopoulos, et al. 2019). For these reasons, external drill-and-fill will be the focus of this upgrade. Drilling from the interior may be preferable in certain situations, such as inclement weather, when siding is difficult to remove, or when the home is vacant. Drill-and-fill insulation Photo by Dennis Schroeder, NLR # 28786 In a drill-and-fill retrofit, small round holes (typically 1- to 2-inch diameter) are drilled into the exterior wall of the home between the studs (e.g., every 16 inches) (U.S. Department of Energy 2022). A hose is inserted into the wall, and insulation is then blown in. Both the small round holes and the hose are visible in Figure 1. Exterior wall studs in residential construction commonly have three widths: 2x3, 2x4, and 2x6. The 2x3 and 2x4 studs are more common in mobile/manufactured homes and older residential construction, whereas 2x6 studs are more frequently used in newer residential construction (Krigger 2006) (Kochkin and Wiehagan 2014). Mobile/manufactured homes may use 2x2 studs, but these are typically only for interior walls (Dickerhoof 1977). This ResStock 2025 Release 1 assumes that R-13 insulation can fit within a 2x4 wall. In cases where higher levels of insulation are installed, OS-HPXML selects the appropriate wall construction set to ensure the desired R- value is achieved. More information on this topic can be found on the ResStock “Wood Stud Depth and Wall R-Value Calculations” page.2 When installing drill-and-fill insulation from the exterior of a building, the cladding material is an important consideration. Exterior wood or vinyl siding is sometimes partially removed to allow holes to be drilled in the exterior sheathing. Wood siding can also be drilled through and then patched. Some types of metal siding may be removable, while others may not be (Allwein and Biddle 2002). In homes with face brick (4-inch) as cladding over wood stud walls, drill-and- fill can be performed by drilling smaller holes through mortar joints. Other construction types, such as concrete masonry units (CMUs) or steel framing, are limited to insulation methods other than drill-and-fill for retrofits (U.S. Department of Energy 2019).
